Need to search first.I could only collect a small part of what you asked for. My research tools hit their usage limit early, before I could open any full page. Everything below comes from search-result extracts of four sources: Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic list), Matthew Henry on Blue Letter Bible (older commentary), Spurgeon on StudyLight (Baptist) and Precept Austin (evangelical). I couldn't read Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Wesley, the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or any Catholic or Orthodox page. So **sections 2 and 3 of your brief are not covered at all**, and some verses have no notes.

**v. 1**
- Elijah simply obeyed God's command. The drought began and ended because God willed it, not Elijah. Elijah's prayers followed God's leading. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry says a man who is true to God will be faithful to his ruler. Obadiah could keep his post at court with a clear conscience, even though he couldn't do all the good he wanted there. Those who fear God don't need to leave a bad world. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm
- Henry finds it striking that Obadiah didn't reform Ahab and Ahab didn't corrupt Obadiah. God has faithful people at every level of society: there were believers in Nero's household and in Ahab's. Same URL.
- Spurgeon traces Obadiah's faith from his youth, through years of steady faithfulness, to outstanding godliness. He finds that all the more remarkable given where Obadiah worked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-kings-18.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Obadiah was a brave man who stood up for God and His prophets in a dangerous time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Henry: Obadiah wasn't content just to fear God himself. He used his wealth and power to protect others who feared God. Bread and water were scarce, yet he kept the prophets alive for later service. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm
- Henry also suggests, as a "perhaps," that Jezebel may have persecuted the prophets on the excuse that they caused the drought. He links the drought to her killing of God's prophets. Same URL.

**v. 5**
- Guzik quotes another writer (the extract doesn't say who): Ahab's only concern was saving his horses and mules. He looked for grass instead of seeking God, and put animals before his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/

**vv. 9–12, 14**
- Guzik: Obadiah knew Ahab had been searching everywhere for Elijah. He feared that if Elijah disappeared again after being reported, Ahab would punish him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Henry: Obadiah thought Elijah wasn't serious about meeting Ahab. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm

**v. 10**
- Henry thinks Ahab wanted to force Elijah to reverse the drought, more than to punish him. He compares this to the superstitious belief that a witch can be made to undo a curse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm

**v. 12**
- Spurgeon suspects Elijah didn't think much of Obadiah. He sees Obadiah as a very cautious man, careful neither to compromise his conscience nor to risk his position, and so a little afraid even of Elijah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-kings-18.html
- Spurgeon uses Obadiah's "from my youth" to preach on faith begun early in life and kept up. Same URL.

**v. 15**
- Guzik: Elijah answered Obadiah's real fears kindly and wisely. He wouldn't make Obadiah die for him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/

**v. 16**
- Henry: Ahab must have been surprised that the man he had searched for so long now turned up without being looked for. Ahab went looking for grass and found the man from whose word he had to expect rain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm

**v. 17**
- Guzik: Ahab, Israel's most ungodly king, blamed the godly prophet. By Ahab's own beliefs this made sense: he thought Elijah had angered the sky-god Baal, who would withhold rain until Elijah was caught and executed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Precept Austin: sadly, Ahab treats God's word through Elijah as the source of trouble, when obeying that word brings peace. After three years he still won't repent and blames Elijah instead. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin sums up what makes someone a "troubler": forsaking the word of the LORD. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary

**v. 19**
- Guzik: Elijah did all this at God's command (he cites v. 36); it wasn't his own strategy. The prophets of Baal had to be dealt with before the rain came, so that everyone would know the rain came from Yahweh, not Baal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Precept Austin notes that vv. 19–20 seem to have all 950 prophets come to Carmel, though only the prophets of Baal are later said to be killed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary

**v. 20**
- Guzik says it's hard to know why Ahab obeyed Elijah. Perhaps he hoped a crowd angry about the drought would turn on the prophet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/

**v. 21**
- Guzik: the Hebrew word translated "waver" (NKJV "falter") means to limp, hop or dance. It's the same word used in v. 26 for the Baal prophets leaping around their altar. So the sense is "How long will you dance between two opinions?" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Guzik: Elijah insisted that serving Baal and serving Yahweh really are different, against the idea that any sincere religion will do. The people's silence meant they would neither defend themselves nor repent. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: their indecision showed in what they did. Same URL.
- Spurgeon: the people's old traditions led them to fear Jehovah, but their interests at court led them to bow to Baal. Many followed Jehovah secretly and half-heartedly while worshipping Baal in public. Elijah aimed his challenge at the waverers, not at the Baal prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-kings-18.html
- Henry, citing Bishop Hall: where God and Baal are truly at war, neutrality is impossible, because whoever is not with God is against Him. The people could neither justify nor condemn themselves, so they said nothing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm
- Precept Austin: there's no partnership between the two masters, between light and darkness or Christ and Belial; you must choose. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-18-commentary

**v. 22**
- Guzik: Elijah had reason to know this wasn't strictly true, since Obadiah had just told him about the 100 hidden prophets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Henry: the verse shows Elijah's courage in standing alone against such power and numbers. It encourages God's witnesses not to fear people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm

**v. 23**
- Guzik: Elijah gave the Baal prophets every possible advantage. He thinks they chose the bulls and decided which one each side would offer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-18/
- Henry: the trial was all the fairer because Baal had every outward advantage. It was gracious of God to let His claim be tested, so that every mouth would be stopped. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_018.cfm

**Not found:** anything for vv. 2, 6–8, 11 and 13. Nothing on where Protestant traditions differ, nothing from modern scholarship or Catholic and Orthodox writers, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. To fill these gaps, a new session would need to open the full Enduring Word and Precept Austin pages and the biblehub.com pages for Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit and Wesley on 1 Kings 18. It would also need the NET Bible notes and Catholic and Orthodox pages on Elijah.
